defaults.permitted_development: A change of use in England depends on the lawful existing use, the proposed use class and any specific permitted development route, not on a general householder right. Many proposals still need planning permission, prior approval or both, especially where external works, servicing or intensified activity are involved. The planning question is usually less about the label of the use and more about traffic, amenity, servicing and the effect on the wider area.

rules.height_rules: There is no automatic height allowance for change of use. Any extra storey, plant, flue, lift overrun or roof equipment is separate operational development and must be assessed in its own right.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth allowance. Rear additions, storage yards, outdoor seating, service areas and enlarged floorspace are separate planning issues from the use change itself.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary effects often decide the outcome: noise, servicing, odour, overlooking, waste storage, deliveries, parking and customer activity can all matter more than the internal use label. The planning question is usually less about the label of the use and more about traffic, amenity, servicing and the effect on the wider area.
rules.roof_rules: New vents, extract systems, plant screens, condensers or roof terraces are not automatically covered just because the use changes. They need their own planning assessment and can be decisive for neighbours.
rules.materials_rules: External alterations such as shopfront changes, shutters, signage, cladding or new openings are assessed separately and should fit both the host building and the wider street scene. The planning question is usually less about the label of the use and more about traffic, amenity, servicing and the effect on the wider area.

rules.permitted_development: In Broxbourne, a technically available change-of-use route can still fail in practice if parking, deliveries and the relationship with adjoining homes are not properly resolved.

rules.height_rules: In Broxbourne, a use change does not carry any automatic roof-level envelope with it, so plant, flues and screens are judged separately and often become the main visual or amenity issue beside housing.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth allowance. Rear extensions, outdoor seating, storage yards, service bays or enlarged floorspace are separate planning issues from the use change itself.
rules.boundary_rules: In Broxbourne, parking, servicing, overlooking and refuse handling at the edge of the site usually matter more than the technical class description.
rules.roof_rules: New extract systems, vents, condensers, plant screens or roof terraces are not covered just because the use changes. They need their own planning assessment and can be decisive for neighbours.
rules.materials_rules: External alterations such as shopfront changes, shutters, signage, cladding or new openings are assessed separately and should fit the host building and the wider street scene. The planning question is usually less about the label of the use and more about traffic, amenity, servicing and the effect on the wider area.

restrictions.conservation_area: Within a conservation area, a change of use is more likely to be assessed alongside frontage changes, servicing, signage and heritage impact, even where the use-class point seems simple.
restrictions.listed_building: Changing the use of a listed building does not remove the need for listed building consent for internal or external works affecting its special character.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove the usual change-of-use fallback route in selected centres or neighbourhoods, so check the property's designation before relying on permitted development.
